conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for coming in today. I’m Maya Bennett, a perinatal mental-health clinician here to support new moms as they navigate all the emotional changes that can come after birth.  

I’d like to spend the next few minutes with the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—better known as the EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question screen that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and mentally over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; this is simply a snapshot so we can be sure you’re getting the support you deserve. Everything we discuss stays confidential within your care team, and you’re welcome to pause or ask questions at any time.  

When you’re ready, we’ll move through each item. I’ll ask the questions conversationally, and you can answer however feels most comfortable.  

Let’s begin:  
Over the last seven days, have you still been able to look forward with enjoyment to things, or has that felt difficult for you?

It’s been… kind of hard, actually. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a quiet bath, even just watching a show I like—but lately those things feel flat. When I think about doing them, I mostly feel tired or like “what’s the point?” I still try, because maybe it’ll help, but the enjoyment part feels pretty far away.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I can still laugh sometimes—like when my husband makes a goofy face to get the baby to smile—but it doesn’t come as easily or feel as good as it used to. Mostly I’m just going through the motions.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I try to tell myself I should be excited about little plans—like when my mom offers to come over or when I think about ordering my favorite take-out—but the spark just isn’t there. It feels more like I’m checking off a box so I don’t disappoint anyone, not like I’m actually looking forward to anything.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah... I catch myself doing that a lot. If the baby’s fussy and I can’t settle him right away, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong or I’m not “in tune” with him. When he wouldn’t latch properly yesterday, I sat there crying, telling myself I’m already failing at the one thing I’m supposed to be good at—being his mom. I know, logically, babies just cry and feeding issues happen, but the guilt still jumps on me.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Almost every day. I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure the baby’s breathing doesn’t sound right on the monitor, even though he’s fine. Or I’ll lie down and my brain starts spinning about whether the diaper rash is actually something worse. There’s no real reason—it just shows up and sits on my chest until I distract myself by checking on him again.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah, that happens too. It’s like a sudden wave—my heart starts pounding, I feel shaky, and I’m convinced something awful is about to happen even though I can’t name what. Last night I was rocking the baby in the dark and out of nowhere I felt this rush of dread, like I needed to run or hide. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me tearful and exhausted.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. It feels like there’s this constant stack of “shoulds”—laundry, bottles, texts I haven’t answered—and every time I cross one off, three more appear. I’ll be feeding the baby and notice the dust on the floor, and suddenly I’m overwhelmed, thinking I’ll never keep up. Sometimes I just sit there paralyzed, staring at the mess, feeling like I’m drowning in stuff that shouldn’t feel so hard.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with everything I didn’t do or might mess up tomorrow. Some nights I drift off okay, then I’m wide-eyed at 2 a.m. listening to every squeak the baby makes on the monitor. Even when he’s sound asleep, I’m staring at the ceiling, feeling this heavy sadness that won’t let me settle.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day, at some point. It’s like a gray cloud that follows me—sometimes lighter, sometimes heavier, but always there. I’ll be changing the baby and suddenly feel this wave of sadness hit me out of nowhere. I end up crying in the nursery more often than I want to admit.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… that’s been happening a few times a week. It’s usually when everything feels like too much—like yesterday when I couldn’t get him to nap and I just sat in the rocker with tears streaming. I tell myself I should be able to handle a baby’s bad day, but the sadness just spills over.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I’m exhausted and overwhelmed, but I’ve never wanted to hurt myself. I just want to feel like *me* again and be a good mom.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary

Patient: Postpartum mother, 2–3 wks after delivery (per history)

Responses on EPDS-10 items:

Symptom clusters endorsed
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, hopelessness (items 7–9)
- Marked anhedonia, loss of anticipatory pleasure (items 1–2)
- Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care (item 3)
- Daily generalized & situational anxiety, panic spells (items 4–5)
- Feeling overwhelmed, “paralyzed,” poor coping (item 6)
- Sleep initiation / maintenance difficulties linked to rumination (item 7)

Safety
- Denies thoughts of self-harm or desire to harm infant (item 10 = 0)

Risk factors
- First-time mother, infant feeding difficulties
- Social support present but perceived pressure to “keep up”
- No suicidal ideation; protective factors include partner involvement, motivation to “feel like me again”

Screening impression
- High likelihood of major postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety features
- Score estimate: ~18–20/30 (formal scoring to be completed)
- Recommends immediate formal psychiatric evaluation, consideration of evidence-based psychotherapy and/or medication, psychoeducation, supports, and safety-planning

Next steps
- Provide patient with crisis line numbers; schedule follow-up within 48 h
- Coordinate with OB / PCP for expedited referral
